segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: I wish you would put up with a little foolishness from me. Yes, do put up with me!

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For I am jealous for you with God’s own jealousy, since I promised you in marriage to one husband, to present you as a pure virgin to Christ.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But I am afraid that, just as the serpent deceived Eve by his cunning, your minds may somehow be corrupted and turned from the sincerity and purity of your devotion to Christ.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For if someone comes and proclaims another Jesus whom we did not proclaim, or if you receive a different spirit that you did not receive, or different good news that you did not accept, you put up with it well enough.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For I consider myself not in the least inferior to these super-apostles.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Even if I am untrained in speaking, I am not untrained in knowledge; in every way we have made this plain to you in all things.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Or did I commit a sin by humbling myself so that you might be exalted, because I announced the good news of God to you free of charge?

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: I robbed other assemblies by taking pay from them so as to serve you,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and when I was with you and in need, I was a burden to no one, for the brothers who came from Macedonia supplied my need. In every way I kept myself from weighing on you, and I will keep doing so.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: As the truth of Christ is in me, this boast of mine will not be silenced in the regions of Achaia.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Why? Because I do not love you? God knows I do.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But what I am doing I will keep on doing, to cut off the opening from those who want an opening, so that in what they boast about they may be found to be just as we are.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For such people are false apostles, deceitful workers, disguising themselves as apostles of Christ.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And no wonder, for Satan himself disguises himself as an angel of light.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So it is no great thing if his servants also disguise themselves as servants of righteousness. Their end will be according to their deeds.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: I say again, let no one think me a fool. But if you do, then accept me even as a fool, so that I too may boast a little.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: What I am saying I am not saying as the Lord would have it, but as in foolishness, in this undertaking of boasting.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Since many boast according to the flesh, I too will boast.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For you gladly put up with fools, being so wise yourselves!

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For you put up with it if someone enslaves you, if someone devours you, if someone takes advantage of you, if someone puts on airs, if someone strikes you in the face.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: To my shame I say that we were too weak for that! But wherever anyone is daring—I am speaking in foolishness—I am daring too.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Are they Hebrews? So am I. Are they Israelites? So am I. Are they Abraham’s offspring? So am I.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Are they servants of Christ? I am talking like a madman—I am more so: in labors far more, in prisons far more, in beatings beyond measure, in danger of death many times.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Five times at the hands of Jews I received the forty lashes less one.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Three times I was beaten with rods, once I was stoned, three times I was shipwrecked, a night and a day I have spent adrift on the deep;

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: on journeys many times, in dangers from rivers, dangers from bandits, dangers from my own people, dangers from Gentiles, dangers in the city, dangers in the wilderness, dangers at sea, dangers among false brothers;

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: in labor and toil, often in sleepless nights, in hunger and thirst, often going without food, in cold and exposure.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Apart from everything else, there is the daily pressure on me: my anxiety for all the assemblies.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is made to stumble, and I do not burn?

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: If I must boast, I will boast of the things that show my weakness.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The God and Father of the Lord Jesus, he who is blessed forever, knows that I am not lying.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: In Damascus the governor under King Aretas was guarding the city of the Damascenes in order to seize me,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and I was lowered in a basket through a window in the wall and escaped his hands.

notes.phrase: Yes, do put up with me!
notes.note: The Greek verb form can be a command (“do put up with me”) or a statement (“but in fact you are putting up with me”). The command is the more common reading and is followed here; the statement is equally possible grammatically and is preferred by some interpreters.

Paul casts himself as the father of a bride, who arranged the betrothal and was responsible for his daughter’s faithfulness until the wedding. Betrothal was a binding commitment, so unfaithfulness in the interval counted as a betrayal of the husband. The picture echoes the prophets’ image of Israel as God’s bride.

notes.traditional: the simplicity that is in Christ
notes.note: Some manuscripts lack the words “and purity”, and older translations based on them omit the phrase. Several of the earliest witnesses include it, and the edition translated here prints it, though scholars are not agreed on which form is original.

The Greek word was an ordinary term for the announcement of good news, used also of public and imperial proclamations. “Gospel” has become a purely religious term or a book title, so the plain meaning is given here, as many modern translations do in places. The related verb in verse 7 is rendered “announced the good news”.

Paul’s phrase is sarcastic, built on a rare adverb meaning “exceedingly”. It is disputed whether he means the rival missionaries in Corinth, whom he calls false apostles in verse 13, or the leading apostles in Jerusalem to whom those rivals may have appealed. The translation leaves the question open.

The Greek word meant a gathering of people, used both for a city’s civic assembly and, in the Greek Old Testament, for Israel gathered before God. “Church” is the near-universal rendering and is not wrong, but it now suggests a building or an institution. “Assembly” is used throughout this translation so the reader can see it is one word.

Most English versions render “in this boastful confidence”. In the Greek of the period the word normally names something objective, such as a plan or project one has taken on, and lexicographers have questioned whether the sense “confidence” is securely attested. The matter is disputed, and the traditional rendering remains defensible.

“Flesh” here stands for merely human standards: ancestry, status and achievements of the kind listed in the verses that follow. It is set against speaking “as the Lord would have it” in the previous verse. Some translations paraphrase as “by human standards” or “as the world does”.

This was a synagogue punishment. The Law of Moses limited a flogging to forty strokes (Deuteronomy 25:3), and Jewish practice stopped at thirty-nine to avoid exceeding the limit by a miscount. The beatings with rods in the next verse were, by contrast, a Roman punishment carried out by a magistrate’s attendants.

The Greek word names armed, violent plunderers such as highwaymen, as distinct from a thief who steals by stealth. “Robbers” is the usual rendering and is not wrong; “bandits” makes clearer the danger travelers faced on the roads.

The Greek word means “peoples” or “nations”; in Jewish usage the plural meant the non-Jewish peoples. This translation renders the same word “Gentiles” or “nations” according to sense. Here it is paired with “my own people”, meaning Paul’s fellow Jews.

notes.traditional: Beside those things that are without
notes.note: The Greek phrase can mean “apart from the things left unmentioned” or “apart from these external things”, that is, the outward hardships just listed. The first is the more common view today, and the rendering here is compatible with it. The word translated “pressure” may alternatively mean the daily stream of people or concerns coming at him.

The verb means to trip someone up so that they fall in their loyalty to God, which is stronger than the modern sense of “offend”. Modern versions vary between “made to fall”, “made to stumble” and “led into sin”. “Burn” most likely means burning with indignation at whoever caused the fall, though some take it as burning with distress.

notes.traditional: the governor under Aretas the king
notes.note: Aretas IV was king of the Nabateans, an Arab kingdom with its capital at Petra, and ruled until about AD 40. The Greek title is “ethnarch”; whether this official governed Damascus for Aretas or was the head of the Nabatean community in the city is debated. Acts 9:23–25 tells of the same escape.

candidates.reason: Paul’s phrase κατὰ σάρκα recurs across his letters and translations vary between “flesh”, “human standards”, “sinful nature” and “the world”, so one policy is needed.
The verb and its nouns run through Romans, the Corinthian letters, Galatians and Philippians, and versions alternate between “boast”, “glory”, “take pride” and “rejoice”, hiding the thread.
The plural recurs throughout the New Testament and a single decision is needed on when it is “brothers” and when “brothers and sisters”, including compounds such as “false brothers”.
This word and ἀφροσύνη need to be kept consistent, and distinguished where possible from μωρός and μωρία, which are also traditionally “fool” and “foolishness”.
The word recurs in Paul (Romans 12:8; 2 Corinthians 1:12, 8:2, 9:11, 9:13; Ephesians 6:5; Colossians 3:22) and is variously rendered “simplicity”, “sincerity”, “generosity” and “single-mindedness”.
